name: Westinghouse WGen7500DF Dual Fuel Portable Generator
summary: The right size and the right outlet for the typical 1/2 to 1 HP well pump plus household essentials.
verdict: The WGen7500DF is the generator most well owners should shortlist first. Westinghouse rates it at 9,500 starting and 7,500 running watts on gasoline, with lower ratings on propane, and it has the feature that matters most for a well: a 120/240V, 30-amp locking outlet (L14-30R) that connects through a power inlet to a transfer switch or interlock kit. That 240-volt output is what most submersible pumps need. By the sizing math in this guide, a 1/2 or 3/4 HP pump is comfortably inside its starting capacity, and a typical 1 HP pump should be within reach, especially if the fridge and freezer are not starting at the same moment. Dual fuel lets you store propane, which keeps indefinitely, instead of relying only on stabilized gasoline. It is an open-frame generator, so it is loud and must run outdoors well away from the house, but for a well pump plus kitchen and lighting circuits it is the sensible middle of the market.
skipIf: Heavy, so it needs wheels and a level spot

name: DuroMax XP13000EH Dual Fuel Portable Generator
summary: Buy it when the pump is 1.5 HP or larger, or when the well has to start while the rest of the house is also running.
verdict: If your pump is 1.5 HP, or a 1 HP pump has to start while the refrigerator, freezer and other motors are also running, you need more surge margin than a 7,500-watt generator offers. DuroMax rates the XP13000EH at 13,000 starting and 10,500 running watts on gasoline, with lower figures on propane, and it includes both a 50-amp 14-50R outlet and a 30-amp L14-30R, both 120/240V. The 50-amp outlet allows a heavier-duty inlet and transfer setup if your electrician recommends one. The extra headroom is what makes pump starts uneventful: the generator's voltage dips less when the motor's locked-rotor current hits, which is easier on both the pump and the generator. The trade-offs are size, weight and fuel. It burns significantly more fuel than a mid-size unit, and moving it requires its wheel kit and a good surface. For a 1/2 HP pump alone it is more generator than you need; for a larger pump, it is the right tool.

name: Champion 9000-Watt Dual Fuel Portable Generator
summary: A strong-value well pump generator if the 240V outlet and starting watts match your pump's sizing table.
verdict: Champion's 9,000-watt dual fuel generator is a popular value pick for well owners because it combines big starting watts, dual fuel and a 120/240V locking outlet at a price that usually undercuts the bigger names. Champion lists 9,000 starting watts on gasoline, with lower output on propane, and the running rating is what you should match against your pump maker's table, so confirm it on the current listing because Champion has refreshed this family several times. For a 1/2 or 3/4 HP submersible on a 240V circuit, it has ample surge. For a 1 HP pump it should work if you stagger other motor loads, letting the pump start before switching on the fridge and freezer circuits. Like the other open-frame units here, it is loud and must run outdoors, away from doors and windows. Champion's broad dealer network and parts availability are a real advantage for a machine that might sit unused for a year and then need to work on the first try.

name: Westinghouse WGen9500DF Dual Fuel Portable Generator
summary: The dual fuel generator to buy if you want real whole-house-adjacent output on either fuel and a 50-amp outlet ready for a proper hookup.
verdict: The WGen9500DF earns the top spot because it loses less on propane than most rivals. Westinghouse rates it at 9,500 running and 12,500 peak watts on gasoline, and 8,500 running and 11,200 peak on propane, a drop of roughly 10 percent where many open-frame units give up 15 percent or more. That matters, because the whole reason to buy dual fuel is to run on propane when gas stations are dark. The panel carries two GFCI duplex outlets, a 30-amp L14-30R and a 50-amp 14-50R, so it works with either a 30-amp manual transfer switch or a 50-amp inlet and interlock. Westinghouse lists run time at about 8 hours on gasoline and 7 hours on a 20 lb propane cylinder at half load, from a 6.6-gallon tank with a gauge. Electric start with a remote key fob is a real convenience. The trade-offs are 211 lb of dry weight and 74 dBA of noise. The standard model has no carbon monoxide shutoff; if that matters to you, and it should, look for the WGen9500DFc, which adds CO sensing.

name: Champion 9200-Watt Dual Fuel Portable Generator with CO Shield (201302)
summary: The best value dual fuel generator for most suburban houses, with CO shutoff built in.
verdict: This is the dual fuel generator most people should price first, and it is the same 9,200-watt class Champion that our home outage guide ranks as its top portable. Champion rates it at 11,500 starting and 9,200 running watts on gasoline from a 459cc engine, enough for a refrigerator, a freezer, a sump pump, a gas furnace blower, lights and Wi-Fi together, with room for a window air conditioner if you stagger start-ups. Like every open-frame dual fuel unit, it makes less on propane, so build your load list from the propane figure on the label, not the headline number. The 7.7-gallon tank gives about 10 hours at half load on gasoline; on propane, Champion lists about 5 hours at half load, so plan on several 20 lb cylinders a day. CO Shield shuts the engine off if carbon monoxide accumulates around it, a backup to good placement rather than a substitute. The panel has GFCI household outlets, a 30-amp L14-30R and a 14-50R that Champion caps at 38 amps. Check the model number before you buy: Champion also sells gasoline-only 9200-watt units.

name: Generac GP7500E Dual Fuel Portable Generator with COsense
summary: A sensible mid-size dual fuel generator for houses with gas heat that need essentials, not everything.
verdict: Not every house needs 9,000-plus watts, and the GP7500E Dual Fuel is the pick for the many that do not. Generac rates it at 7,500 running and 9,400 starting watts on gasoline, and 6,800 running and 8,500 starting on LP. That is enough for a refrigerator, a freezer, a sump pump, a gas furnace blower, lights and a window air conditioner with sensible staggering. Generac's PowerRush feature is designed to boost starting capacity for motor loads, which helps with pumps and compressors. COsense monitors carbon monoxide around the unit and shuts it down if levels climb. Generac lists up to 10 hours at half load on gasoline from a 7.9-gallon tank, and 5 hours on a 20 lb LP cylinder. The panel has two GFCI duplex outlets and an L14-30R, and Generac describes it as transfer switch ready, so it matches a standard 30-amp manual transfer switch or 30-amp inlet. What you give up is the 50-amp outlet and the extra headroom of the 9,500-watt class, and it is still 204 lb. If your load list fits under about 6,500 watts on propane, it is the simpler buy.
